# Uncertainty and survival analysis: generated by `uq_survival.py`

Two additions to the RUL model, both aimed at questions the point prediction cannot answer:

- **Conformal prediction:** how wrong can "23 cycles left" be, with a guarantee attached? And does alarming on the safe end of that range help?
- **Survival analysis:** a real fleet has few failures and many engines still running. Can the running engines be used instead of thrown away?

## Part A: conformal lower bounds

A one-sided **90% lower bound** on remaining life: "at least X cycles left", true 90% of the time. One-sided because over-predicting life is the dangerous error. Calibrated with 5-fold cross-conformal (CV+) grouped by engine, so every training engine contributes an out-of-fold residual. Scored on 20 held-out engines per sub-dataset (every cycle) and on the official test set (one point per engine).

| sub-dataset | method | coverage, held-out engines | coverage when true RUL < 25 | coverage, official test set | average margin (cycles) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FD001 | quantile GBM, not calibrated | 79% | 56% | 73% | 8.4 |
| FD001 | split conformal | 89% | 99% | 86% | 13.8 |
| FD001 | Mondrian (per band) | 90% | 91% | 87% | 14.3 |
| FD001 | CQR (conformal quantile) | 89% | 89% | 84% | 11.4 |
| FD002 | quantile GBM, not calibrated | 90% | 79% | 84% | 11.8 |
| FD002 | split conformal | 93% | 100% | 90% | 15.5 |
| FD002 | Mondrian (per band) | 95% | 94% | 91% | 16.0 |
| FD002 | CQR (conformal quantile) | 94% | 91% | 90% | 14.0 |
| FD003 | quantile GBM, not calibrated | 90% | 64% | 70% | 6.9 |
| FD003 | split conformal | 95% | 100% | 87% | 11.5 |
| FD003 | Mondrian (per band) | 95% | 88% | 84% | 9.9 |
| FD003 | CQR (conformal quantile) | 96% | 95% | 84% | 9.3 |
| FD004 | quantile GBM, not calibrated | 90% | 78% | 79% | 10.9 |
| FD004 | split conformal | 91% | 84% | 89% | 14.7 |
| FD004 | Mondrian (per band) | 91% | 76% | 89% | 13.0 |
| FD004 | CQR (conformal quantile) | 94% | 95% | 87% | 12.4 |

**Reading it.** Averaged over sub-datasets, the calibrated bounds cover 92% (split), 93% (Mondrian) and 93% (CQR) of held-out cycles against a 90% target. The uncalibrated quantile model, which was *trained* to be a 10th percentile, covers only 87%: the calibration step is what makes the number true.

**Near failure (true RUL < 25), where the alarm decision is made**, the three differ. Split conformal over-covers (96%): one correction sized for the noisy healthy region is too wide where the model is sharp. Mondrian, calibrated per band of *predicted* RUL, comes in under target (87%, and 76% on FD004), because an engine the model wrongly thinks is healthy sits in the wrong band. **CQR holds up best here (92%)**, because its width comes from the sensors, not from the prediction.

**The official test set comes in lower** (88% / 88% / 86%). That is a limit of what the method promises: the guarantee holds for points drawn the same way as the calibration points (every cycle of an engine's life). The test set takes one point per engine at a random cut-off, which over-samples mid-life. Mid-life (the knee where wear starts) is where coverage is lowest on the held-out engines too (true RUL 50-125: 86% for CQR), so that is the likely reason. A guarantee is only as good as the match between calibration and use.

### Does alarming on the lower bound help?

`split` and `Mondrian` compute the bound from the point prediction alone, so alarming on the bound is identical to moving the threshold on the prediction. Only **CQR** can alarm earlier on an *unusual* engine than on a typical one with the same prediction. The fair test compares policies at the **same average warning** (the same amount of engine life thrown away) and asks which one protects the worst engines better.

Pooled over 80 held-out engines, persistence k and threshold searched per signal:

| average warning | point prediction: engines missed / worst engine | CQR lower bound: engines missed / worst engine |
|---|---|---|
| ~15 cycles | 6 / 0 cycles | 0 / 10 cycles |
| ~20 cycles | 3 / 0 cycles | 0 / 13 cycles |
| ~25 cycles | 1 / 1 cycles | 0 / 16 cycles |
| ~30 cycles | 1 / 5 cycles | 0 / 20 cycles |
| ~40 cycles | 0 / 20 cycles | 0 / 27 cycles |

*Missed = less than 10 cycles of warning, or none. Worst engine = the least warning any single engine got.*

**The safety question, asked directly: how much average warning does each signal need before no engine is missed?** The point prediction needs **31.9 cycles**; the CQR lower bound needs **16.5**. Same safety, **15.4 fewer cycles of engine life thrown away per engine** (bootstrap over engines: 95% CI 4.5 to 17.4, positive in 99.8% of resamples).

Why: the point prediction is confidently wrong on a few unusual engines. To catch those, a plain threshold has to fire early on *every* engine. CQR widens the safety range only where the sensors look unusual, so it can fire early on those engines and late on the rest.

**Out of sample.** The numbers above pick each policy on the same engines they score. Choosing the policy on a random half and scoring it on the other half (200 splits): point prediction misses 1.38 of 40 engines on average with 27.4 cycles of average warning; CQR misses 1.22 with 15.7. The saving survives: similar misses, 11.7 fewer cycles thrown away. **But neither reaches zero misses on engines it has not seen** (75% / 68% of splits miss at least one). A policy tuned to "no misses" on 40 engines is not a no-miss policy; a real safety case needs a margin on top.

On the *worst 5%* of engines (rather than the worst one) the gain is smaller and not significant: CQR minus point = +2.2 cycles at ~20 [95% CI -1.0, +10.0]; +3.9 cycles at ~30 [95% CI -1.0, +12.0]. The benefit is concentrated in the few engines the point model gets badly wrong, which are exactly the ones that decide a safety case.

Under the project's default cost model, the best point-prediction policy costs 1.55 per engine (RUL<49, k=8, 0.09 false alarms per engine) and the best CQR policy 1.18 (bound<15, k=3, 0.10 false alarms per engine).

## Part B: survival analysis on a censored fleet

Each training fleet is cut down so only *n* engines are observed to failure; every other engine is still running, observed up to a random point in its life (right-censored). Everything, including the sensor normalisation, is refitted on what that fleet has actually seen. Scored on the official test set.

Six ways to use that fleet:

1. **GBM, drop running engines.** What the rest of this repo does: no label, no row.
2. **GBM, treat running engines as failed.** The trap: pretends every engine failed the day observation stopped.
3. **Weibull, failed engines only.** A survival model without the extra data (the control).
4. **Weibull, with running engines.** Weibull accelerated-failure-time model on landmark data, using the censoring properly.
5. **GBM + survival-imputed labels.** Running engines get the label the survival model expects *given that they survived at least this long*: E[min(RUL, 125) | still running, sensors]. The GBM trains on real labels plus these.
6. **Same, Weibull fit on failures only.** Separates the value of the censoring logic from the particular fitted curve.

Test RMSE, mean ± sd over seeds (lower is better):

| sub-dataset | failures seen | GBM, drop running engines | GBM, treat running engines as failed | Weibull, failed engines only | Weibull, with running engines (censored) | GBM + survival-imputed labels | GBM + imputed labels (Weibull fit on failures only) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FD001 | 5 of 100 | 23.5 ± 1.4 | 39.1 ± 1.0 | 21.6 ± 1.5 | 25.9 ± 1.4 | 23.2 ± 1.1 | **20.3 ± 1.3** |
| FD001 | 10 of 100 | 21.2 ± 1.7 | 37.6 ± 0.8 | 21.0 ± 0.8 | 23.5 ± 2.1 | 19.4 ± 1.3 | **18.4 ± 0.3** |
| FD001 | 20 of 100 | **15.2 ± 0.9** | 33.2 ± 2.0 | 18.5 ± 0.5 | 19.7 ± 0.8 | 16.0 ± 0.8 | 15.3 ± 0.3 |
| FD002 | 5 of 260 | 25.3 ± 5.1 | 40.5 ± 1.1 | 25.2 ± 1.8 | 44.7 ± 4.8 | 38.4 ± 4.6 | **21.2 ± 0.8** |
| FD002 | 10 of 260 | 20.3 ± 2.7 | 39.3 ± 0.8 | 20.8 ± 0.4 | 30.6 ± 2.4 | 25.4 ± 2.5 | **16.9 ± 0.4** |
| FD002 | 20 of 260 | 16.4 ± 0.9 | 36.2 ± 0.4 | 18.3 ± 0.6 | 24.0 ± 0.7 | 19.9 ± 0.5 | **15.3 ± 0.1** |
| FD003 | 5 of 100 | 21.9 ± 3.2 | 39.8 ± 1.4 | 27.5 ± 1.1 | 37.1 ± 3.8 | 31.1 ± 3.3 | **21.7 ± 0.6** |
| FD003 | 10 of 100 | **20.0 ± 3.4** | 38.3 ± 1.2 | 24.4 ± 0.9 | 27.6 ± 2.7 | 23.8 ± 2.0 | 20.7 ± 1.1 |
| FD003 | 20 of 100 | **15.7 ± 0.8** | 31.5 ± 0.7 | 22.2 ± 1.4 | 23.1 ± 2.4 | 18.4 ± 1.4 | 17.6 ± 1.5 |
| FD004 | 5 of 249 | **30.3 ± 5.5** | 40.0 ± 1.0 | 38.6 ± 9.6 | 51.8 ± 2.6 | 45.7 ± 5.2 | 33.5 ± 11.9 |
| FD004 | 10 of 249 | 23.9 ± 1.3 | 39.6 ± 1.9 | 29.2 ± 3.2 | 38.5 ± 4.3 | 32.6 ± 3.0 | **22.8 ± 0.8** |
| FD004 | 20 of 249 | **19.4 ± 1.3** | 37.7 ± 0.8 | 25.0 ± 1.3 | 31.9 ± 0.9 | 25.7 ± 0.6 | 20.3 ± 1.0 |

Reference with **every** engine run to failure (the luxury C-MAPSS normally gives): FD001 GBM 12.5 / Weibull 17.1, FD002 GBM 13.1 / Weibull 15.7, FD003 GBM 12.9 / Weibull 18.5, FD004 GBM 14.4 / Weibull 22.3.

Averaged over sub-datasets:

| failures seen | GBM, drop running engines | GBM, treat running engines as failed | Weibull, failed engines only | Weibull, with running engines (censored) | GBM + survival-imputed labels | GBM + imputed labels (Weibull fit on failures only) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5 | 25.2 | 39.9 | 28.2 | 39.9 | 34.6 | 24.2 |
| 10 | 21.4 | 38.7 | 23.8 | 30.1 | 25.3 | 19.7 |
| 20 | 16.7 | 34.6 | 21.0 | 24.7 | 20.0 | 17.1 |

**What it shows.**

- **Treating running engines as failed is the worst option at every fleet size** (39.9, 38.7, 34.6 RMSE). It teaches the model that healthy engines are about to die. More data used wrongly is worse than less data.
- **The method that works: a Weibull fitted on the failed engines, used to fill in labels for the running ones** ("given it has survived this long, how long is left?"), then a GBM trained on all of it. Averaged over sub-datasets it beats dropping the running engines at 2 of 3 fleet sizes (RMSE reduction: +1.0 at 5, +1.6 at 10, -0.5 at 20 failures seen; negative means worse). It is the single best method in 7 of 12 cells and beats dropping in 7 of 12. The gains are modest (1-2 RMSE when failures are scarce, none at 20), but it is also **steadier**: seed-to-seed spread 1.7 vs 2.3 RMSE for dropping. With 5 failures, which 5 you happened to see matters a lot when the other engines are thrown away, and much less when they are used.
- **Why the failures-only fit, not the one that also saw the running engines.** The running engines still contribute: the label each one gets is conditioned on how long it has already survived, which is the censoring information. What they should not do is shape the fitted life curve, for the reason in the next point.
- **The Weibull on its own gets worse, not better, when the running engines are added** (better at 0 of 3 fleet sizes). The model is the bottleneck: log-life linear in the sensors, one shape for every engine. Running engines are mostly early-life rows and outnumber the failures, so they pull the straight line toward the healthy region and it becomes optimistic late in life. Letting the shape vary with the sensors (ancillary regression) was tried and did not fix it. The survival model is useful here as a *label generator* for the GBM, not as the predictor.
- **C-index** (does the model rank which engine fails first correctly; 0.5 is chance): 5 failures: GBM-drop 0.813, imputed 0.810; 10 failures: GBM-drop 0.832, imputed 0.839; 20 failures: GBM-drop 0.855, imputed 0.854.

**Limits.** Censoring here is random (each running engine is cut at a uniform point in its life). Real censoring is not random: engines that reach failure are the ones maintenance missed. `complete.py` stage 8 models that bias for the drop-the-running-engines baseline; it is not re-run here. Three seeds per cell is enough to see the direction, not to rank close methods.

Wall time: 47.3 min.
